pages.html:
anna: The most interesting thing for me about how the project came about was that I didnt chose to work in the bingo hall Camden Arts Centre chose the bingo hall and then chose me to work there as an artist. then I did the rest at camden and I got in touch with you during that time because I knew that youd already done a project about bingo with Jane......

karen: with Jane and also with Lawrence

anna: ......and we'd talked about that before. so for me you were like the bingo expert

karen: also I was going to bingo at the time as a punter

anna: were you? but you're not now?

karen: no

anna: why's that?

karen: I got sick of it

anna: because of the project?

karen: partly yeah and also because it ran it's course with me really - it stopped being fun and it stopped being exotic I suppose which is part of it's charm for me...
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
anna: in a nut shell I ended up viewing the project as being in 3 phases with the residency being the first phase, which was predominantly spent doing a progression of events at camden arts centre. These were to do with finding out about the project and exploring different possibilities and working with different people centred around gambling and religion - what are the connections between gambling and religion. and going to the state so being in both places at once; and the idea of bringing the art audience in at the beginning of a project instead of at the end and doing things back to front - presenting the audience with the research stage of the project

karen: and also bringing the bingo audience into the art space

anna: well thats what we did with eyes down can you describe the eyes down day in a nut shell

karen: we sent invites to people at the state and people through camden arts centre and I remember it was billed like we proudly present Saturday bingo so it was a bingo game at the camden arts centre where we kind of mixed traditional bingo business with other stuff that had been talked about and gathered through your work at camden arts centre - through talks and work with people like thomas and amy and me......

anna: and stuff youd already done on your own and with jane - I remember you brought your madonna in a scallop shell and other stuff from las vegus

karen: and so we used the format of a traditional old fashioned bingo...
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
anna: sort of village style wasn't it?

karen: yeah like town hall or village hall bingo

anna: and there were easter prizes

karen: yeah it was easter wasn't it

anna: so there was already that religious link

karen: and we had that old bingo machine which was full of coloured balls. It was like a big cube and you'd switch it on to activate the wind effect and all these ping pong balls would fly about and go up a shoot and each of the balls has a number and then you get a ball come up the shoot and you call the number out...

anna: it's like pool backwards isn't it

karen: kind of ... so we had that and we gathered loads of used bingo books from the state and we got really into that whole thing of how people mark their bingo books - the difference expressions

anna: like angry pens - manic scratching like drawing

karen: yeah it was mark making - very expressive mark making and how people make the anonymous grid of the bingo card their own that's very personalised ...
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
anna: and they write prayers on the back sometimes don't they - there's one that really sticks in my head 'god bless these pages'

karen: yes and 'help me' was another and then people's funny little number systems written on the back and there was one with names of relatives as well

anna: and appeals to the caller - george

karen: as well as a couple of really abusive ones like 'george you wanker' and stuff like that, so we gathered all those up, we covered the windows of the room as well.......

anna: the room was quite churchified

karen: .... we all made them stained glass effect

anna: yes we all did that - we did that together

karen: yeah - it took ages all that stained glass and we had fairy lights

anna: oh and we made our own bingo books out of those blue flyers and we called them 'miracles' - 'faith' - 'hope' - 'wish' so there was the wish game the 'miracle game' and the 'hope game' wasnt there?
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
karen: and the prizes were all easter themes so it was very like a church hall bingo and me and justine went out with a tiny budget and got easter wishing eggs and

anna: kinder eggs - that whole thing of surprise and wishing and how that's connected. It is quite fascinating how those threads run through so much - through every thing somehow

karen: we had pound coins wrapped up in lottery slips, oh, and a box of eggs with that inside as well

anna: oh I have to diverge - even though I know were not allowed to - but earlier this year I went to bingo as part of another project in a village hall in cumbria with a few other artists who were involved in the project and it was quite funny because it was like anna'll know how to play and of course i'd forgotten coz Im so bad with numbers I was like aah don't ask me - but the only thing we one was 2 dozen eggs it was really weird - one of those funny things

karen: yeah - coming back full circle. Yeah, so we had all that and we put the prizes on a table with fairy lights all round so making it a magical fairy grotto in a slightly poor tacky kind of way but it had a real festive feel about it and there were tables cloaked with bingo books...
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
anna: I remember also bingo players from the state who came in a mini bus with Shaun and I remember them teaching people from the art world how to play bingo which was a really nice moment. There were people who came who'd never been to a gallery before and might never go again so that was quite nice as well - this kind of transportation of one world to the other which ran through the project as well

karen: yeah and vice versa for one day - .......that was it really it was quite straight forward just me calling the games

anna: and Shaun facilitating

karen: and I remember actually going out of that room. I ventured out with my microphone to drum up business and we had that sandwich board outside

anna: and every one was looking at the Sophie Calle show

karen: that's right yeah and nobody was coming in and we weren't sure what to do about it so I went out started saying 'come on in ladies and gents don't be shy' trying to get them in and feeling really weird about that

anna: doing something in an art gallery that's not art is a bit like going into a church and doing something that you shouldn't be doing in church - it's such a designated space.
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
karen: and because it's a mixed audience it's perceived differently by different people in the audience

anna: which is quite unnerving I mean exiting about that work was that there were always people involved that were seeing things in totally different ways and as the producer of those different meanings it's quite scary it's like - wow it's a can of worms and somebody could really misunderstand it or understand it in ways wed never thought of - which is very interesting.

karen: I think thats the most important thing actually is the dual role

anna: of the project?

karen: and us as individuals within that. On the one hand being seen as somebody whos a bingo caller and on the other as a performance artist

anna: thats interesting about collaboration in that everyones framing everyone else. like if were collaborating with each other were also collaborating with camden arts centre and theyre collaborating with state and were collaborating with state were all collaborating with our audiences etc. etc. it's like everyones framing everyone else all the time - it is quite confusing and interesting

anna: Shall we talk about gambling - addiction - belief that whole thing - and mecca and what happened there - we became kind of on site therapists.
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
karen: thats more role playing isnt it

anna: yeah artists as this that and the other - I loved the fact that sean - mecca customer services - offered you a job calling bingo at the state after the special event - seeing you as a performance artist because hed been to art school

karen: really? did he go to art school? I didnt know that

anna: didnt you know that?

karen: no

anna: yeah sean went to art school. he left mecca after the project and went on....

karen: have you been in contact with him

anna: no, and niethers he - but your role was really brilliant in that it was really being between performance art and saying I want to be a bingo caller

karen: yeah really blurring boundaries

anna: and the fact that you played with that real desire that was a fantasy but became real in a fictional way because it was part of an art project but also in a real way because you were offered a job.
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
anna: It reminds me a bit of when I was doing the pony race project and people were asking me afterwards are you gonna do one next year? kind of interesting moment where you realise that what starts as a fiction or a proposal or an art work becomes surreal for other people as well as just you which is really great somehow

karen: and doesn't happen very often when youre making work that is event based or performance based your creating a happening rather than a thing but that is quite an unusual thing in that it extends beyond that moment and that context - it doesnt happen very often that it spreads beyond that and as you say it becomes something that is very real in a different way

anna: it's like that you can insert a little bit of fiction into a situation and that can bleed out and become real - like merging. I guess were doing that the whole time thats what reality is or something. I wish id never said that - well have to edit out definitions of reality! .....

..... anna:: I was very impressed when you told me that youd paid for your degree show partly by betting on the horses - thats fantastic - do you remember when you showed me how to put on a bet and I one money on another nightmare

karen: another nightmare oh gosh yeah

anna: and we went for lunch

karen: on the proceeds - see it can pay
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
anna: oooh yes yes but thats yes and weve talked a lot about the link between addiction and gambling and numbers and systems and compulsion and stuff and that was what was so nice about us both reading BLA...... actually coz thats so what it was about. in a way we share something. some part of our personalities are really obsessive - getting stuck to something in a certain way that feels like we understand each other on that level very very well do you know what I mean?

karen: yes yes

anna: im not sure I want to state myself as a compulsive obsessive

karen: weve talked about that though specifically about compulsive obsessive behaviour and systems that we both constructed as children which is quite interesting like the counting thing and

anna: I did cracks in the pavement on the way to school every day - missing them

karen: missing them I did the very same thing I think thats a common one

anna: counting in your head

karen: counting in your head and doing things......

anna: I used to do the alphabet actually
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
karen: ..... like even though I knew how many drawers there were - 4 - in the chest of drawers by my bed I still had to keep counting them. I had a fear of just stopping in my sleep just sort of dropping dead for some reason so I did this thing a sort of reassurance like a mantra I suppose over and over and over again

anna: but thats just to do with an ordering and classifying and stuff like and it feels like thats another thing weve had to do through out this project has been to try and order and classify what a few minutes before weve just mushroomed out through conversation coming up with lots of material lots of ideas and then weve gone right - how are we going to categorise that? how are we going to order it? it's like the conversations with the questionnaires and then spending hours honing it back down to a sort of system of all the images and then hours spent finding them all - going to covent garden and going to the library - generating and sourcing images thats a kind of strange part - maybe that part of that process which me feels to me like a very normal way to work isnt necessarily normal at all

karen: do you think it's not? it feels normal to me

anna: well I don't know maybe it's just something to do with artists I mean normals a crap word - shouldnt use it really. it's about being in control and losing control and the dynamic between the two - gamblings got to be about that
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
karen: yes and thats what we talked about particularly with bingo that it's the most controlled form of gambling because there is this very set ridged little grid that you never move away from and numbers the numbers are very safe in themselves - safety in numbers -

anna: that was going to be some running theme to something wasnt it - but yeah there a number is a number

karen: though of course numbers go on and on to infinity

anna: strangely Im very dyslexic with numbers - numbers make me panic

karen: but within bingo 90 is the highest number you cant go beyond ninety and theres a great safety in that and the whole ritualised stuff around bingo is that it's very repetitive very and that really came across in the questionnaires and with talking to people

anna: thats why theyre into it

karen: thats why they go

anna: it's a safe place

karen: everything about it is safe they know whats going to happen every time and the only thing that is going to possibly defer from the routine is that they might win - well they already know that somebodys going somebody always has to but very rarely them
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
anna: and the anecdotes that popped out were of people cheating the system do you remember there were really funny storeys about - well I cant really remember them now but some really unusual events. it is a kind of extraordinary way of controlling surprise it's like a trickle a sort of drip feed of excitement it's like stimulation and excitement in very small doses on a regular basis every day it's drugs in a way or it makes me think of drugs or sort of makes me think of that thing of buying more chances. like if you buy more books you buy more chances to win - I don't know why that just popped into my head again and people keep going back for 20 years and spend quite a lot of money - obviously it's prioritised everyone prioritises what to spend their money on but that came across more with the fruit machine players actually but thats more of an addiction

karen: thats more dangerous - not controlled is it

anna: yeah bingo is amazingly safe

karen: I suppose you could buy books and books and books and books and books but theres more or less a limit to how much

anna: how many you can play at the same time - there was a woman who played 12 books at a time wasnt there but I think she was a myth - she was myth

karen: she was a bingo legend - myth

anna: alt goddess bingo superwoman
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
karen: what really came across to me just talking to people was the regularity of it and people came and spent a lot of money - these were mainly people who possibly don't have that much control in their lives generally people who don't have much disposable income

anna: people who cant do that many things and make many decisions and it's deciding and making decisions that gives you a sense of control over your life and destiny. well wasnt bingo brought to britain for uk housewives in the 60s? where did I get that from? that that was how it started - from the states. I mean it existed before but as a social club idea and if you think about it housewives in the 60s didnt have any power for various reasons

karen: well they certainly didnt have any economic power and people who go there now generally don't have much economic power

anna: and social power

karen: it's linked isnt it

anna: yes who was it that said where else can I go? I cant go a park alone and I cant go to a pub alone I don't even want to go to a cafe alone I feel awful I don't want to sit on my own and thats changed but still yeah that was really moving - just being yeah but where? the world is really not built for women on their own in their 60s they get approached or seen or stigmatised....
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
karen: I know because I had that problem when I was doing my bingo project a couple of years before I wasnt allowed to take film or even still photographs I had to do it sneakily

anna: that informed the whole project and then it changed

karen: and then it changed the whole advertising thing making it glam girls on a night out fun kind of thing and it's marketed to appeal to a younger people and that interesting that camden were seeing it in that way as a fun thing

anna: initially they were

karen: initially well the bingo hall up the road which I don't think you ever came to with me you know the beacon the new competition - the purpose built - is very like all the adverts very glitzy glammy a lot of neon full of young people always packed the contrast between that and the state and camden picked the state and If they wanted a fun glam project they should have picked the beacon. the state is very much old fashioned bingo and the audience are very much the traditional older people mainly women some men but mainly women fairly sort of disenfranchised people in a way

anna: I was thinking of that word disenfranchised and the image of the cigarette smoke and darkness it was like this beautiful art deco cinema - chandeliers velvet carpets really stunning - is a weird counter point to someone sitting down for six hours or standing at a fruit machine
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
karen: theres a huge poignancy in that whole place

anna: it's kind of abject glam

karen: completely

anna: yeah it's a has been. I remember going there the first few times with you and thomas and just thinking it's all here isnt it somehow - so much already. maybe thats how we decided to work - not doing a big thing - do you remember? which was to not do a spectacular intervention type thing. not coming in and saying hello heres some art were putting some art in the bingo hall because in a way the whole thing already is something and then the idea of the projection - 30 days in june of projections - not being it but I don't know I think that part was misunderstood stood. the purpose of that was to lead to talking mecca - it was to lead to more conversation

karen: which it didnt

anna: well weirdly it was invisible - the work ended up being an invisible project -apart from the special event......

karen: thats quite interesting

anna: .....which I feel ambivalent about anyway - whats interesting the fact that it was invisible?

karen: yes
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
anna: yes that is very interesting. do you remember talking about doing a huge projection of the virgin mary really early on

karen: yes

anna: and also we talked about wanting to do a miracle - I really liked

karen: I really liked that idea that idea

anna: but it had to reveal it'self to us and it never did

karen: I think the budget restricted the.....

anna: what the miracle?

karen: well yes because the miracles that people were asking for were real miracles you impossible like they were things like my mother coming back from the dead or my husband being cured of cancer or

anna: daughter getting pregnant

karen: yeah or monetary things like getting a huge win on the national game and being able to go round disney land in florida and take friends all round london in a stretch limo. people didnt really look for little miracles which I think we were hoping for - which was a bit foolish really - god if youre gonna want a miracle you gonna want something big arent you
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
anna: I remember spending a week where I looked for good luck and bad luck or I noted down when good luck happened to me or bad luck happened to me which was very easy to do coz it fitted my kind of compulsive -lets make a list in my head of whats happening - from things like just cycling through a puddle. trying to split every experience into a good luck or a bad luck thing which was like small miracles in a way and it was kind of like sensitising yourself

karen: which is what everyone was doing everyone was sensitised to that and completely tuned into superstition utterly in every tiny way

anna: like the thing happened to me today so I think I might win tonight

karen: and the woman who if somebody was sitting in her seat would turn round and give her books back and go home - and having to use a certain pen and so on do you remember the woman who if she knocked one leg shed get bad luck and if she knocked two legs shed get good luck

anna: we saw five black cats the other day

karen: did they cross your path

anna: they were all around us

karen: were you freaked out

anna: I sort of thought god whats this?
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
karen: shit

anna: yeah

anna: I remember feeling weirdly responsible at one point that someone might think wed affected their winning or losing which was interesting in terms of art - ie youre meant to have an effect - and weirdly not wanting to and maybe thats why part of the work was so invisible

karen: completely - thats the problem always - wanting your presence felt and at the same time not wanting to impose and intrude which is always a difficulty when youre taking work......

anna: if your in someone elses space

karen: in someone elses space always whatever youre doing .........but if youre taking work out of a gallery into non art public space then thats always an anxiety

anna: whos territory are you in

karen: you have to be really aware of limitations and particularly there because it is so full of limitations and rituals and rules and thats something that I was interested in myself - I was fascinated by the world of bingo

anna: the construction of the bingo world

karen: and that once you're in there it has it's own codes and it's own language and it's own iconography and de de de
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
anna: it's a game - no clocks no windows no time

karen: exactly and thats something I find fascinating about going into other worlds the racing world as well has it's own codes language rules and de de de

anna: you are all playing a game together it's like church you go into that space together - and art galleries - and you all agree to abide by certain rules and so were all gonna smoke our heads off and sit on our own and be quite friendly to each other on the whole in this space in a way that we cant be in the street - it's an institution in a way it's what institutions are all about

karen: exactly yeah

anna: why is that so enticing do you think for you? is it security do you think a sense of knowing where you are

karen: partly - oh god why is it?

anna: for me it's about wanting to belong

karen: I think it is about wanting to belong but for me it's about the excitement of entering into a world where you don't entirely belong - that you have an insight into the customs and the language and the de de de so that you can act within that

anna: you can pretend

karen: you can pretend - you can play - it's about playing
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
anna: thats about playing with your identity isnt it and playing with the idea that you can transform yourself into somebody else which has got to be a really important ingredient in life

karen: well thats why we go on holiday really isnt it partly and that is something which is quite important for me to do in my fantasy world anyway in my imaginative world something that ive always done. so it was a very different feeling from going there and just slotting in - I mean youve got partly your observers hat on because youre not entirely in that world you don't go 3/4 times a week. you can dip in and out of it....

anna: and your not hooked

karen: ....but thats very different to how we went into it as artists - that was quite hard for me actually

anna: I found that so uncomfortable. the other day I found some notes id written about it like usually I try to write a diary when im doing a project and one of the opening sentences in it was something like: I cant bare saying the words we're doing an art project ever again it's just so like - so what?

karen: that was an issue - why are we doing it? who are we doing it for?

anna: why are we doing it here? - someones idea at camden arts centre 3 years ago. but I found the hard core extreme aspect of not wanting to do it and people not wanting it and people asking why put art into a space like this? ....
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
.... anna: a really interesting aspect of the project. but I do really like the idea of the projections coming form the conversations and being like apparitions and like someone saying to gabby ooh I think I saw a horse down by the cafe and that it did work on a certain scale but it was odd because it was almost like theatre - trying to do a theatrical illusion show over a long period of time and we didnt want to tell people anything about it

karen: we didnt want to announce it

anna: it was like we wanted people......

karen: to notice it stumble on it or not

anna: ......to have apparitions. and I remember talking to you about being worried that someone might freak out and some one said put the lucky numbers at the top of the stairs and I thought he shouldnt have said that someone might fall down the stairs

karen: george said that

anna: he was great wasnt he - dead pan - he thought it was a load of crap. what was his name for me?

karen: kate - key hole kate from the beano or something

anna: what name id he give you

karen: I don't think he did I don't think I had a name - missy or something
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
anna: I felt like the subject was endless and the projects not finished and in a way it never can be because the subject is too endless and it was like dipping in to something I suppose and what remains out of that is the fact that people did connect enter into dialogues exchange information and talk a bit and thats it really - thats all that remains somehow

karen: yes which is why it's important to do this

anna: the web site

karen: yes something beyond that - I mean it's a bit hard to leave isnt it? how did you feel about having this very involved relationship with the place and all those people and then just going?

anna: awful I felt really awful. I remember getting a lift with anne and her son to kilburn high road and just giving her a huge hug and feeling like she was my mum and then just getting on the tube and ive never been back after a year of being there - after several months of going there almost every day. well as you know there was always meant to be a kind of conclusion follow up re-presentation and this is it - it is going to happen finally. I like the fact that you don't finish a project and put it to bed and I like the idea that nothing really ever ends but in practice on an emotional level you need to complete things and say goodbye to people and have a kind of little ceremony - we should do a funeral for the project!! - thats a real ingredient of working with other people because you do form relationships and some you carry on and some you don't and it does bring up that thing of were all from different worlds which are more than the comparisons between our individual lives but we all live in quite different social worlds even if we live just down the road from each other. and age - it's like you meet people when you do something but if their 20 years older than you and youve got nothing in common youre not going to see them again - so maybe thats a miracle. what did you feel?
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
karen: oh when I left? well the same really - just really......

anna: dangling?

karen: yeah ......and I felt really guilty about it actually and I just thought should I go back and just say hi to people then I thought I don't know what my role is

anna: well we made promises we said we were going to make a book thats whats lead to this as well - a determination to do something you cant just lie to people no way there was exchange there

karen: oh definitely that was how we got people to talk to us

anna: on talking mecca on the second stage of talking mecca

karen: yeah that we would be putting together some kind of book thats why people actually came and spoke to us

anna: amy took the dummy there actually and showed people

karen: oh right but that was something that I remember us talking about - that it would be nice to give something back and to make something actually physical something material out of the time there instead of ethereal stuff

anna: it was time wasnt it time spent conversations had little exchanges by fruit machines and all sorts of those things that become part of your life I mean I guess one of the ideas through that project - I don't know what I think about it now - was that the whole process of doing the project and being there over 9 months is in a way like performance art. so my presence, your presence, peters presence, any one connected with the mecca project was kind of becoming a performance artist. ...
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
... anna: it's an idea although I know it's not perceived as that but I quite like thinking about it in those terms the minute you start being there and ask a question the art starts happening - whatever that is - maybe you need to do that in a more pure way for that to become very clear. someone did a north london link project - he did that in finchley road he just talked to people for three days and defined that

karen: I think you do need to define it

anna: mecca went on for so long which is great it refuses definition in a really nice way it's like fuck you im not gonna become a thing

karen: I think youre right I think thats a role that you do take on when you do any kind of work that has a life or a making an event happen or whatever. because what some people perceived as the work was the projections and of course it wasnt that and those were really documentation in a way

anna: they were documentations of images from conversations about something else.

karen: but the conversations were more like the work so it and the images were documentation and

anna: and we also talked about those images as spurs or sparks to start new conversations between people and I also remember talking about them as on-wall art kind of tongue in cheek were just putting pictures on the wall but they were only ever there for half a second so it was playing with that idea of - and im sure I remember people saying to us the artists when are you putting the pictures up?
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
karen: oh they did - like where are the paintings?

anna: how do you think the mecca projects fed into other stuff? if it has or do you feel like when you've completed it youll be able to process it more

karen: yeah I think so because I still feel it's just hanging isn't it?

anna: I feel like that as well. when people have asked me about it I've gone into that real panic mode of aaagh I can't open that cupboard coz all these boxes are gonna fall on my head

karen: I cant think what to say about it really

anna: yeah it was a naff question at this stage

karen: the side line that I found quite amusing and frustrating at the same time was this expectation from people that art and wealth must be equated that people might have been thinking we got paid really well for doing this like you can just come along to a bingo hall and just chat to people for a living

anna: or you're students

karen: or you're students yeah

anna: well the mythology around the art world - I don't blame them. I mean look at how the media represent art. it's like were all pop stars taking drugs all the time or were starving in the garrets. it's good to meet people and undo that and say well no we get paid a bit but not very much and we do other stuff as well and it's part of our lives and were not students. we covered so many roles in 'talking mecca' from the researcher to the photographer to the interviewer to the therapist and organiser.
pages.caption: Karen and Anna

pages.html:
.... anna: there was a wonderful morning when I was in the managing director of the State's chair - before he came in to work - on his phone organising and we had just taken over their office and they were wonderful the staff were amazing letting us. that was another interesting thing - us inserting our production of an art project into the daily production of the bingo business. That felt quite exciting at times because they really let us in - here's the code to the office door, you can use the video player, the computer, the photocopier etc. Ann said that we were like therapists but that's what people who sit around and listen are - what did that make you think?

karen: I felt a little uncomfortable about it because we weren't therapists and in a way I felt that we were being fraudulent - we were wanting something from people

anna: didnt we tell them though?

karen: yes we did but again it's that blurring of boundaries and roles and relationships. I mean it's a fairly solid stand point you know come and talk to us - were doing this book which is a fairly solid thing and it's a respectable thing in the eyes of a lot of people for some reason....

anna: it's printed

karen: .....and then people just really opened up some people much more than Id expected to be continued...
pages.caption: Karen and Anna
